CausalChain: Tumor cells under intrinsic stress and altered metabolism produce extracellular vesicles loaded with immunomodulatory factors -> these EVs are secreted into the circulation (STIE) where they are taken up by peripheral immune cells (e.g., T cells and dendritic cells) -> EV-delivered cargo upregulates immunosuppressive molecules (e.g., TGF-β, IDO) and exhaustion markers (e.g., PD-1) in these cells -> This induces T cell exhaustion and regulatory T cell expansion, compromising effective anti-tumor responses in the tumor microenvironment (TIME) -> The immunosuppressive TIME reduces the efficacy of PD-1 inhibitors in solid tumors
Hypothesis: Inhibiting the release or cellular uptake of tumor-derived extracellular vesicles can reverse the systemic and local immunosuppressive effects, thereby restoring T cell functionality and enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of PD-1 blockade in solid tumors.
Abstract: We propose that tumor‐derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) play a pivotal role in reprogramming the systemic tumor immune environment (STIE) by transferring immunomodulatory molecules, including non‐coding RNAs and proteins, to circulating immune cells. This transfer promotes T cell exhaustion and the expansion of regulatory T cells, ultimately supporting an immunosuppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) that undermines the efficacy of PD-1 blockade. Targeting EV biogenesis, release, or uptake may counteract these effects and enhance the response to immunotherapy.
